clue.text: Long to have hands embracing girl with a file on her?

definitions.text: girl with a file on her?

indicators.note: embracing means the pair of hands wraps around the word for longing

parts.note: the two hands are right and left, R and L
to long for something is to ache for it

explanation.surface: Someone yearns to hold a girl who is the subject of a dossier.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition points to Martin Amis's novel The Rachel Papers, whose narrator keeps a file on his girlfriend.
explanation.definitionFit: Martin Amis's novel The Rachel Papers is named after the dossier its narrator compiles about the girl he pursues.

clue.text: Laundry equipment is lighter after removing its top

indicators.note: the first letter is cut off the comparative word for paler in colour

parts.note: lighter in shade is fairer

explanation.surface: A clothes-drying rack weighs less once its upper part is taken off.
explanation.definitionFit: A clothes horse or rack for drying washing indoors is laundry equipment.

clue.text: Bit of weed smuggled in coat for Dr. Gonzo, say

indicators.note: smuggled in means one piece is slipped inside the other

parts.note: a coat of paint is a layer

indicators.note: a bit of the word weed is its opening letter

explanation.surface: A scrap of cannabis hidden in a jacket belongs to Hunter S. Thompson's drug-fuelled companion.
explanation.walkthrough: Dr. Gonzo is the attorney in Hunter S. Thompson's Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas; 'say' marks him as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Dr. Gonzo is the narrator's attorney in Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas, an example of a legal professional.

clue.text: A lady concealing plot to get one of The Carpenters

indicators.note: concealing means the titled woman's word holds the garden plot inside it

parts.note: a lady of rank is a dame
a plot of garden is a bed

explanation.surface: A woman hides a scheme to win over a member of the pop duo.
explanation.walkthrough: The Carpenters suggests the pop group; George Eliot's title hero is a carpenter.
explanation.definitionFit: George Eliot's title character is a village carpenter, so he is one of the trade.

clue.text: Hotel yarn with no plot maddened a man of letters

indicators.note: maddened means driven wild, so these letters are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: A plotless story set in a hotel drove a writer to distraction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'maddened' rearranges HOTEL, YARN, NO and PLOT; 'with' only joins them.
explanation.definitionFit: The Victorian novelist of Barchester was a prolific author, and a writer is a man of letters.

clue.text: Artist upset by big counterparts of Burns and those new on the scene?

indicators.note: in a down clue, upset means the abbreviation for an artist is turned upside down

parts.note: RA is a Royal Academician, an artist
a burn is a Scottish stream, so big counterparts of burns are large watercourses

explanation.surface: A painter is troubled by large versions of the Scottish poet and by newcomers.
explanation.walkthrough: Burns looks like the poet, but a burn is a Scottish word for a stream, whose big counterparts are rivers. 'upset' turns RA into AR.
explanation.definitionFit: People who have just arrived are newcomers to the scene.

clue.text: What is stolen by outlaw, a former member of the IRA

definitions.text: a former member of the IRA

indicators.note: is stolen by means the query word is taken inside the word for prohibit

parts.note: to outlaw something is to ban it
eh is an exclamation meaning what?

explanation.surface: Something is taken by a bandit who once belonged to a republican paramilitary group.
explanation.walkthrough: Brendan Behan, the Irish playwright, joined the IRA as a youth. 'outlaw' is a verb, not a bandit.
explanation.definitionFit: The Irish playwright Brendan Behan was jailed as a teenage volunteer of the Irish Republican Army.

clue.text: "These — he heap'd with glowing hand / On golden dishes and in baskets bright / Of wreathed silver: sumptuous they stand" (Keats)

parts.words: "These — he heap'd with glowing hand / On golden dishes and in baskets bright / Of wreathed silver: sumptuous they stand" (Keats)
parts.note: a fill-in quotation from The Eve of St Agnes: the missing word names the dainty foods Porphyro piles on golden dishes

explanation.surface: Lines from Keats's The Eve of St Agnes with one word blanked out for the solver to supply.
explanation.walkthrough: A literary fill-in: in The Eve of St Agnes Porphyro heaps a feast of fine foods for Madeline; the solver supplies the missing noun.
explanation.definitionFit: The quoted lines need a plural noun for choice, dainty foods piled on golden plates.

clue.text: Advice for the dehydrated author of Mary Stuart

definitions.meaning: someone short of fluid should be told to take a glass of the clear stuff
John ..., English poet and playwright, wrote the play Mary Stuart

explanation.surface: Tips for thirsty people come from a playwright about a Scottish queen.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone short of fluids is told to have a glass of H2O; the playwright John of that surname wrote Mary Stuart.

clue.text: Student digs female writer tried for obscenity

definitions.meaning: a ... of residence is university student accommodation
Radclyffe ... novel The Well of Loneliness was prosecuted for obscenity in 1928

explanation.surface: A woman author on an obscenity charge lodges in university housing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'digs' is British slang for lodgings.
explanation.definitionFit: Students often live in a residence building; Radclyffe of that surname wrote The Well of Loneliness, which was banned.

clue.text: Flowers cut and given to love? He's a charmer!

indicators.note: cut means the final letter is trimmed off the verb for thrives

parts.note: flowers as a verb means thrives or prospers
love is zero in tennis, the letter O

explanation.surface: A bouquet trimmed and offered to a sweetheart wins over a romantic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flowers' is a verb, thrives, not blooms in a vase.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's magician in The Tempest casts spells, and a charmer is one who works enchantments.

clue.text: European visiting very pleasant city of Aschenbach's demise

indicators.note: visiting means one piece goes to stay inside the other

parts.note: pleasant means nice

explanation.surface: A traveller from Europe calls on a delightful place where a famous character died.
explanation.walkthrough: Gustav von Aschenbach dies in Thomas Mann's Death in Venice.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Mann's novella has its writer hero Gustav von Aschenbach die in the Italian lagoon city.

clue.text: English and French men start to admire Hartfield's mistress

parts.note: MM is short for messieurs, French for gentlemen

indicators.note: start to means only the opening letter of the next word is taken

explanation.surface: An Englishman and Frenchmen begin to admire the lady of a country house.
explanation.walkthrough: Hartfield is the Woodhouse family home in Jane Austen's novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Austen's heroine Miss Woodhouse is the lady of the house at Hartfield.

clue.text: Low son with attitude pinching knight's diamond

indicators.note: pinching means the run of pieces grips the chess abbreviation inside it

parts.note: to low is to moo like a cow
tone means manner or attitude
N is the chess notation for knight

explanation.surface: A lowly boy with a bad attitude steals a nobleman's gem.
explanation.walkthrough: Wilkie Collins's novel takes its title from a stolen Indian diamond. 'Low' is the cow's call, not humble.
explanation.definitionFit: In Wilkie Collins's novel the title gem is a yellow Indian diamond, and the name is also a gemstone.

clue.text: Lad seen around a jolly place visited by Crusoe

indicators.note: seen around means the young man's word is placed about the other pieces

parts.note: a lad is a youth
a jolly is old slang for a Royal Marine, RM

explanation.surface: A boy is spotted near a cheerful spot that a castaway called at.
explanation.walkthrough: 'jolly' is not cheerful but naval slang for a Royal Marine. Robinson Crusoe sails from Hull and is nearly wrecked off Yarmouth Roads.
explanation.definitionFit: Defoe's hero puts in at the Norfolk port early in Robinson Crusoe, so it is a place he visited.

clue.text: Individual urged to haul in line as Captain Ahab was

parts.note: one means a single individual
egged on means urged

explanation.surface: A single person is pressed to pull in a rope, like the captain hunting a whale.
explanation.walkthrough: In Moby-Dick, Ahab lost a leg to the white whale and walks on an ivory peg.
explanation.definitionFit: Melville's captain has an ivory peg in place of the limb the whale bit off.

clue.text: A despicable sort on a hill is Dougal Douglas?

parts.note: git is British slang for a contemptible person
a tor is a rocky hill, as on Dartmoor

explanation.surface: A nasty piece of work stands on a hilltop.
explanation.walkthrough: Dougal Douglas is the disruptive Scot who stirs up trouble in Muriel Spark's The Ballad of Peckham Rye.
explanation.definitionFit: Spark's Dougal Douglas stirs up unrest among Peckham's workers, an example of a troublemaker.

clue.text: Polish horse associated with The Queen and a man of note?

parts.note: to hone is to sharpen or polish
gee-gee, GG, is a childish word for a horse
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the Queen

explanation.surface: A Polish horse is linked with royalty and a celebrity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Polish' looks like the nationality but is the verb. A man of note is a composer: Arthur Honegger, Swiss-French.
explanation.definitionFit: Arthur Honegger, the Swiss composer of Pacific 231, wrote music, so he is a man of musical notes.

clue.text: Language used in stanzas endlessly

indicators.note: endlessly means the first and last letters come off the word for stanzas

parts.note: stanzas are verses

explanation.surface: A tongue employed in poetry without end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endlessly' strips VERSES of V and S; 'used in' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: Erse is an old name for the Gaelic tongue of Scotland or Ireland.

clue.text: Damage from use in centre of classier blinds

indicators.note: in means the word for damage goes inside the letters picked out
the centre of the word classier is its middle two letters

parts.note: wear is deterioration through use

explanation.surface: Wear and tear shows in the middle of some posher window shades.
explanation.walkthrough: 'blinds' is a verb here, from 'eff and blind', to curse, not window shades.
explanation.definitionFit: To eff and blind is British slang for cursing, so blinds means curses.

clue.text: Ultimately hate good man cuddling my Suzie Wong?

indicators.note: ultimately means the last letter of the next word is taken
cuddling means the saint abbreviation wraps round the exclamation

parts.note: a saint, ST, is a good man
cor is a British exclamation like my!

explanation.surface: In the end, a virtuous man hates hugging a famous fictional woman.
explanation.walkthrough: Suzie Wong, of Richard Mason's novel The World of Suzie Wong, is a Hong Kong bar girl.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard Mason's Suzie Wong works as a paid companion in a Hong Kong bar, so she is an example.

clue.text: Old socialist enthralling a mountain nymph

indicators.note: enthralling means captivating, so the socialist's word holds the article inside

explanation.surface: An old left-winger is captivated by a spirit of the hills.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth an oread is a spirit of the hills and peaks.

clue.text: Self-exiled writer trashed new car in French article

indicators.note: in means the shuffled letters sit inside the French article

parts.note: le is a French definite article

indicators.note: trashed means wrecked, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An author living abroad wrecked a new vehicle in France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trashed' scrambles the new car, and 'in' places those letters within the French article. Lawrence left England in 1919 and lived abroad thereafter.
explanation.definitionFit: D. H. Lawrence left England in 1919 and spent his remaining years wandering abroad by choice.

clue.text: Fool written about by Bond's left in charge

indicators.note: in means the letter for left sits inside the word for charge

parts.note: something in your charge is in your care

explanation.surface: A clown described by the spy has been left in control.
explanation.walkthrough: Bond is the dramatist Edward Bond, not 007: his play The Fool is about the poet John Clare. 'Bond's' stands for 'Bond is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Edward Bond's play The Fool dramatises the life of the peasant poet John Clare.

clue.text: Augustan satirist training to pen artistic composition

indicators.note: to pen means to enclose, so the training letters hold the other piece

parts.note: PE is physical education, training
op, short for opus, is an artistic work

explanation.surface: A satirist of the Augustan age practises writing a work of art.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pen' looks like writing but means enclose.
explanation.definitionFit: Alexander Pope, author of The Dunciad, was the leading satirist of the Augustan age of English verse.

clue.text: Poetic sort of myth, saga or novel

indicators.note: novel means new, so these letters are given a fresh arrangement

explanation.surface: Poetry as a kind of myth, saga or novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' looks like another genre in the list but signals the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: The author of the Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard was an eighteenth-century poet.

clue.text: Dope and gun found in case of detective Maigret?

parts.note: gen is slang for information, dope

explanation.surface: Drugs and a firearm are discovered in an investigation by a famous detective.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dope' is information, not drugs; Simenon's Maigret is a French policeman, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Simenon's Maigret is a French police officer, an example of a policeman in France.

clue.text: Port from Australia picked up for seminal critic

explanation.surface: A harbour in Australia is noticed by an influential literary reviewer.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Philip Sidney's An Apology for Poetry is a founding work of English criticism.
